scope: Reported, not verified legal status. Measures affecting data centers / large loads, battery energy storage and EV charging, as reported by the linked source on the date it was read. Coverage is incomplete: no record never means no restriction. Not legal advice.
method: Hand-curated from primary public sources (legislature, municipal and commission pages) and news reports; a source link, its publisher and the date it was read are on every record. No compiled commercial tracker is a source.

records.title: PSC procedures for reviewing Alabama Power contracts with large-load data centers under Act 2026-610
records.summary: The commission unanimously adopted procedures under which each covered Alabama Power data center contract is filed with a public summary and a confidential financial submission. A contract is deemed approved if commissioners do not vote within 90 days.
records.note: News source only; the docket number and effective date are not given. The procedures as reported cover Alabama Power only. TVA-served areas are outside PSC jurisdiction.

records.title: HB 399 (2026), Act 2026-573, tax abatements for data processing centers
records.summary: For abatements granted on or after 1 January 2027, caps the data processing center abatement period at 20 years, with a possible 10-year extension tied to continued local investment. It stops certain state tax abatements once the largest data centers are placed in service, sends that revenue to the General Fund, and extends the incentive law's sunset to 31 July 2032.
records.note: News coverage of the Senate companion (SB 265) gives 100 MW or more as the size at which state sales and use taxes apply. Confirm that threshold against the enrolled act.

records.title: SB 270 (2026), Act 2026-610, PSC review of utility contracts with large load data centers (Code of Alabama §37-4-22.1)
records.summary: Sets the standard for Public Service Commission review of retail electric contracts with data centers of 150 MW or more expected peak demand. A contract is in the public interest if its pricing and terms are expected to recover the incremental cost of serving the customer and bring positive benefits to other ratepayers.
records.note: Covers only customers that meet the data processing center definition in §40-9B-3 and operate solely for data processing. It is a cost-allocation standard, not a siting rule.

records.jurisdiction: State of Alabama (Association of County Commissions of Alabama resolution)
records.title: ACCA resolution asking the Legislature to recognise county planning and zoning authority in unincorporated areas
records.summary: County commissions unanimously approved a resolution asking the Legislature to formally recognise county land-use authority in unincorporated areas. It says most counties cannot lawfully adopt even a temporary data center moratorium; lawmakers may take this up in the 2027 session.
records.note: No bill exists. This matters for due diligence because most Alabama counties lack zoning power outside city limits, so county-level pauses may be unenforceable.

records.title: 180-day zoning moratorium on data centers and renewable energy projects
records.summary: County commissioners approved a 180-day moratorium, effective immediately, during which the county will not accept or review rezoning requests or permits for new data centers and renewable energy projects. Single-family permits on existing lots and already-approved projects are unaffected.
records.note: News source only. statusDate is the report date; the vote was 'last week' (early October 2026), so 180 days runs to roughly early April 2027. The source does not say which parts of the county are covered or whether battery storage counts as a renewable energy project.

records.title: County commission resolution opposing data center development
records.summary: In June 2026 commissioners passed a resolution opposing data center development, citing energy costs, water, air quality, noise, infrastructure and wildlife. It has no legal force because the county lacks zoning authority.
records.note: News source only; the exact date in June 2026 is not given. It is non-binding, a signal of local opposition and not a prohibition.

records.title: One-year moratorium on bitcoin mining and data center development
records.summary: The county commission adopted a one-year moratorium pausing a proposed bitcoin-mining data center while it reviews zoning and noise standards. A state senator plans a local bill next spring to give the county authority to permit or regulate data centers.
records.note: Enforceability is doubtful: Alabama counties generally lack zoning authority in unincorporated areas, and the planned local bill reflects that. The project is near Somerville. The town's own moratorium was reported in search results but not verified.

records.title: Project Marvel rezoning (about 670 acres to light industrial)
records.summary: Over sustained public opposition, the council voted 5-2 to rezone roughly 670 acres to light industrial for Project Marvel. The campus is planned at about 4.5 million sq ft and is projected to draw about 1,200 MW.
records.note: News source only. The vote date is inferred from 'Tuesday night' and the 2025-11-20 article date. A 2026 request to rezone about 900 more acres was reported in search results but its outcome was not verified.

records.title: Zoning text amendment making data centers a permitted use in I-1 light industrial
records.summary: The council voted 6-0 to add data centers as a permitted use in the I-1 light industrial district and to reclassify several parcels from A-1 agricultural to I-1. This cleared the way for Project Marvel and later data center proposals.
records.note: News source only. The vote date is inferred from 'Monday evening' and the 2025-10-08 article date. No development standards are reported.

records.title: 180-day suspension on considering new data center proposals
records.summary: The City Council enacted a 180-day suspension on considering new data center proposals while it drafted zoning rules.
records.note: Treat as historical. A 180-day term from 2026-03-03 runs to about 2026-08-30, and the council adopted its data center zoning ordinance on 2026-06-09. No source confirms the exact end date. The Nebius project in Oxmoor Valley was exempt. Expiry date computed from the stated term and start date, not stated by the source.

records.title: Data center zoning ordinance (size classes and hyperscale standards)
records.summary: The council voted 6-3 for an ordinance that classes data centers by size and sets standards for each. Hyperscale sites (over 200,000 sq ft or over 30 MW) need closed-loop cooling, a 5-acre minimum lot, 500 ft from residential zoning, 1,000 ft from fixed-guideway transit, noise studies, and on-site generation limited to solar and fuel cells except in emergencies.
records.note: News source only; the ordinance number and effective date are not given. A special-exception (public hearing) requirement was removed before passage. It does not apply to the already-permitted Nebius project. Applies inside city limits.

records.title: One-year moratorium on new data centers
records.summary: The council approved a one-year moratorium on new data centers, alongside a separate one on rental residential communities, to give staff time to write zoning standards.
records.note: News source only; the tally and ordinance number are not given. Applies inside city limits. The county is from general knowledge, not the article.

records.title: Resolution No. 2026-116, temporary moratorium on data center applications
records.summary: The council paused accepting, processing and approving applications to develop, build, expand or operate data centers inside city limits while it updates zoning. A separate proposed ordinance (No. 2026-42) that would ban data centers was not acted on, pending Planning Commission referral.
records.note: The Tribune does not give the length; 256 Today and CBS 42 report one year. Watch Ordinance No. 2026-42 (outright ban), whose status after referral was not found.

records.title: Six-month moratorium on data centers, cryptocurrency mining facilities and server farms
records.summary: On final reading the council adopted an ordinance halting, for six months, the acceptance, processing and approval of applications for data centers, Bitcoin and cryptocurrency mining facilities, server farms and similar uses. The city will use the time to revise its zoning, environmental and design rules.
records.note: The ordinance number and end date are not stated; six months from adoption is about early March 2027. The city-owned utility, Riviera Utilities, reportedly already requires data centers to bring their own power.

records.title: Six-month moratorium on data center development pending new zoning rules
records.summary: The council unanimously adopted a six-month moratorium on data center development while the Planning Commission drafts zoning rules. The ordinance being drafted would also regulate battery energy storage systems, which the current code does not address.
records.note: News source only. The moratorium covers data centers, not BESS; BESS is tagged because the pending zoning ordinance would regulate it. The city reported one battery storage inquiry. Six months from adoption is about mid-December 2026, but no end date is stated.

records.title: Temporary moratorium on data center development
records.summary: The council approved a temporary moratorium on data center development while staff and the Planning Commission study zoning, operating, buffering and infrastructure standards. The city says it has no pending data center applications.
records.note: statusDate is the date of the city's post; the adoption date and ordinance number are not stated. The city gives no length, while CBS 42 reports up to one year. Applies inside city limits.

records.title: One-year moratorium on data center campuses and similar high-impact facilities
records.summary: The council voted unanimously for a one-year pause on property development and permit approvals for data center campuses and similar high-impact facilities.
records.note: News sources only. The vote date is inferred from 'Monday night' and the 2026-06-09 article date. Applies inside city limits. The county list is from general knowledge of where Leeds sits, not from the sources.

records.title: Work-session discussion of a dedicated data center zoning district
records.summary: At a council work session, officials directed staff to recommend which zoning district could allow data centers and how to regulate them, possibly by adding a new zone. Recommendations go to the council, then the Planning and Zoning Commission, before any ordinance.
records.note: The headline says leaders rejected a moratorium, but the article text reports no formal vote. No data center is currently proposed.

records.title: Moratorium on new data centers
records.summary: The council passed a moratorium on new data centers. The council's attorney said it will not apply to the Edged project on Telegraph Road because that developer applied first; the developer has threatened to sue if its building permit is blocked.
records.note: News sources only. statusDate is the report date; the adoption date and length are not stated. Search results conflict on length (six months versus 480 days first proposed); verify with the city clerk.

records.title: 12-month moratorium on data centers
records.summary: The council approved a 12-month moratorium on data centers as a precaution. No developer has approached the city.
records.note: News source only. statusDate is the report date; the vote date, tally and measure number are not given.

records.title: APSC affordability and cost-containment docket (reported as Docket 26-042-U), including large-load tariffs
records.summary: The commission opened a generic docket on customer affordability and cost containment that asks for comment and testimony on large-load tariffs, time-of-use programs and performance-based ratemaking. All Arkansas utilities are parties.
records.note: The docket number is uncertain: this source lists 26-042-U, while an Arkansas Business article seen only in search results gives 26-043-U. Opening date and schedule were not found. The source is a trade association summary, not the APSC docket.

records.title: Docket 22-026-TF, Order No. 8: utility-owned public EV fast charging (Entergy Arkansas Rate Schedule 66)
records.summary: Authorizes investor-owned utilities to install and own public DC fast chargers, with conditions: site hosts may meter electricity sold at a station, vendors come from a pre-qualified list, and utilities file annual reports. Entergy's tariff for its own public fast chargers of 50 kW and up took effect under the order.
records.note: The order's issue date was not found; February 10, 2023 is the tariff's effective date on the filed sheet. The order itself was not opened.

sources.publisher: U.S. DOE Alternative Fuels Data Center

records.title: Entergy Arkansas–Google special rate contract for the West Memphis data center, and amended contract
records.summary: Arkansas has no data-center-specific large-load tariff; large customers are served under individually negotiated special rate contracts reviewed by the PSC. Entergy and Google sought approval of the West Memphis contract in September 2025 and filed an amended, sealed contract in October 2026 that the commission is due to hear in January.
records.note: Pending refers to the amended contract. Approval of the original contract in December 2025 was reported in search results but not confirmed in an opened source, and no docket number was found. Contract terms are largely redacted. News sources only.

records.title: Act 373 of 2025 (SB307): Generating Arkansas Jobs Act of 2025
records.summary: Utility law that lets utilities begin recovering financing costs for new generation and infrastructure through a rider while it is under construction. Reporting describes it as the vehicle for building plants that partly serve large loads such as the Google data center.
records.note: The legislature's page gives the title and act date only; the description of the rider and its use for Entergy's $1.6 billion Cypress Solar project comes from the news source, which does not cite the act number.

records.title: Act 493 of 2025 (SB416): repeal of the Electric Vehicle Infrastructure Grant Program and Fund
records.summary: Repealed the state's Electric Vehicle Infrastructure Grant Program and the fund behind it, removing a state funding source for charging station deployment.
records.note: A funding change, not a siting or sale-of-electricity rule. No Arkansas statute on who may sell charging or on per-kWh sales was found in this search.

records.title: Act 548 of 2025 (HB1444): amendments to the data center sales and use tax exemption
records.summary: Amended the 2023 sales and use tax exemption for data centers.
records.note: Only the bill title and act date were verified. Secondary summaries (not opened) say it cut the minimum investment from $500 million to $100 million, added a multi-site large data center tier and excluded crypto mining; confirm against the act text before relying on those details.

records.title: Act 819 of 2023 (HB1654): sales and use tax exemption for data centers
records.summary: Created sales and use tax exemptions for qualifying data centers, covering equipment, certain services and electricity used by the data center.
records.note: Qualification thresholds were not read from the act text. Amended by Act 548 of 2025 (next record).

records.title: Act 851 of 2023 (HB1799): Arkansas Data Centers Act of 2023
records.summary: Created a state framework for data centers and digital asset mining and preempted cities and counties from adopting ordinances that discriminate against those businesses. Local officials and reporters read it as barring outright local bans on data centers.
records.note: The effective date is from news coverage. This act is the legal backdrop for every 2026 Arkansas local moratorium: officials in Pulaski County, Little Rock and Fayetteville have said it limits bans but not regulation. Amended in 2024 (next record).

records.title: Acts 173 and 174 of 2024 (SB78, SB79): amendments to the Arkansas Data Centers Act on digital asset mining
records.summary: Two emergency acts amended the 2023 law: one bars foreign-party-controlled ownership of crypto mines, the other sets up state regulation of digital asset mining. Together they are reported to require noise-reduction measures and state permits, add civil penalties, and return some regulatory authority to local governments.
records.note: The legislature's pages give titles only, and secondary sources differ on which act holds which provision, so the two are reported together. Per the law-firm summary, the Oil and Gas Commission's permitting rule (Rule K) took effect February 23, 2025, and a federal judge preliminarily enjoined Act 174 and Rule K on April 30, 2025; the foreign-ownership provisions were also restrained in December 2024. Check current litigation status.

sources.publisher: KUAR / UA Little Rock Public Radio

records.title: SB60 (2025): prohibit digital asset mining within 30 miles of a military facility
records.summary: Would have amended the Data Centers Act to bar crypto mining businesses from locating within 30 miles of a military facility. It was amended and sent back to the Senate City, County and Local Affairs Committee, where it died at sine die adjournment.
records.note: Never voted on by either full chamber.

records.title: SR11 (2026 fiscal session): resolution to allow a bill requiring advance notice before data center or mining land purchases and construction
records.summary: Would have opened the way for a bill requiring companies to notify state regulators and local governments at least six months before buying or leasing property or starting construction for a data center or digital mining facility. It failed of adoption and died at adjournment April 29, 2026.
records.note: The official title refers to digital asset mining businesses; the Extension summary says it covers data centers as well.

records.title: SR7 (2026 fiscal session): resolution to allow a bill changing digital asset mining requirements and local government authority
records.summary: A Senate resolution by Sen. Bryan King to permit introduction of a non-budget bill amending the Data Centers Act on noise, water and electric strain and on local governments' authority over these businesses. It failed of adoption on third reading and died at adjournment April 29, 2026.
records.note: The sources differ on its local-control direction: the Extension summary says it would limit local authority, while a search-result description (not opened) said it would return power to local governments. Read the resolution text before characterising it. Companion resolutions SR8, SR9, SR10 and SR12 on crypto mining also failed; they may be refiled in the 2027 regular session.

records.title: October 2023 crypto mine noise ordinance struck down (Jones Digital v. Arkansas County, No. 2:23-cv-220)
records.summary: The Quorum Court passed an ordinance in October 2023 setting a 45 dBA night limit and notice duties aimed at one crypto mine operator. A federal court enjoined and struck it down as discrimination barred by Act 851, and the case closed with an amended consent decree on May 1, 2024.
records.note: Rejected here means invalidated by a court, not voted down. The source is a law-firm analysis; the court documents were not opened. It is the leading example of Act 851 being used against a local ordinance.

records.title: Data center and crypto mining noise ordinance for unincorporated Benton County (2023)
records.summary: The Quorum Court voted 11-3 to regulate data centers, including crypto mines, in unincorporated areas. Noise reduction is required at 65 dB or more in the daytime and 55 dB or more at night, measured at the receiving property line by a third-party acoustic engineer.
records.note: Passed days before Act 851 took effect on August 1, 2023, and modelled on an Association of Arkansas Counties draft; the county judge said 35 of 75 counties had passed similar ordinances. Vote date inferred from the report's reference to Thursday. News source only.

records.title: 12-month moratorium on high-impact industrial and high-intensity digital infrastructure facilities
records.summary: The Quorum Court unanimously passed an emergency ordinance pausing data centers, AI computing facilities and crypto mining for one year, effective on passage.
records.note: Ordinance number not stated; one year from passage is about June 16, 2027. News source only.

records.title: Five-year moratorium on new data centers
records.summary: The Quorum Court unanimously adopted a five-year moratorium on data centers, the longest in Arkansas at the time. No project was pending in the county.
records.note: Vote date inferred from the report's reference to Monday. An end date of August 31, 2031 appeared in search results but was not confirmed in an opened source. The county also banned wind turbines for three years in October 2025. News source only.

records.title: Three-year moratorium on data centers, digital asset mining and large-scale server operations
records.summary: The Quorum Court approved a moratorium through August 31, 2029 on data centers, digital asset mining businesses and other large computer or server operations, to give officials time to study the industry and write regulations.
records.note: Vote tally not reported; two public hearings preceded the vote. News source only.

records.title: Ordinance 26-OR-19: requirements for high-intensity digital infrastructure uses (data centers)
records.summary: Classifies large data centers in unincorporated areas as heavy industrial uses needing a conditional use permit. Applicants must show no undue burden on grid, water and infrastructure, meet noise limits, keep 500 feet from residential property, and provide a decommissioning plan with financial assurance. It passed 11-4 on September 22, 2026, was vetoed, and the veto was overridden 10-4 on October 27.
records.note: AVAIO Digital (ADP Little Rock Data Hub LLC) sued in the U.S. District Court for the Eastern District of Arkansas about October 29, 2026 to block it; the ordinance has no carve-out for AVAIO's project near Wrightsville. The September passage date is inferred from the report's reference to Tuesday. Ordinance text was not opened.

records.title: Proposed one-year data center moratorium (failed May 26 and July 28, 2026)
records.summary: A one-year pause on new data centers was first announced as passed on May 26, 2026, but a recount showed 8 votes where 10 were needed for the emergency ordinance. A second version exempting projects already under way failed on July 28, leaving the county with no moratorium.
records.note: Some aggregator headlines still say Pulaski County enacted a 12-month moratorium; that is wrong. The county instead adopted permanent regulations in October 2026 (next record).

records.title: One-year pause on data centers (June 2026)
records.summary: The Quorum Court adopted a one-year pause on data centers in June 2026.
records.note: Status date is the report date. The source gives only the month and length; vote date, tally, scope and ordinance number were not found. News source only.

records.title: Data center ordinance (June 2026) and ten amendments (August 18, 2026)
records.summary: A June 2026 ordinance put data centers under conditional use review with water and electricity impact reports, setbacks, buffers and generator rules. On August 18 the council voted 7-0 for ten further changes tightening noise protections, limiting water and energy use and raising penalties.
records.note: The June adoption date and the ordinance text were not found. The August vote date is inferred from the report's reference to Tuesday. No data centers currently operate in the city. City limits only. News sources only.

records.title: Board review of data center development rules (study session requested July 21, 2026)
records.summary: City directors asked for a review of data center rules, including possible limits on water use by regional water customers, for an August 11, 2026 study session. Under a 2023 zoning change, data centers need conditional use approval in Industrial Light zones and are allowed by right in I-2 and I-3.
records.note: No moratorium or new ordinance had been adopted as of the report, and the outcome of the study session was not checked. Status date is the report date. News source only.

records.title: Data center regulation ordinance (adopted June 2, 2026)
records.summary: The Board of Directors unanimously adopted citywide data center rules covering noise, landscaping and utility requirements and barring groundwater or drinking water for cooling. As proposed by the mayor, hyperscale sites (250,000+ sq ft and over 50 MW) are confined to industrial zones at least 1,000 feet from non-industrial property, with noise caps of 70 dB by day and 65 dB at night.
records.note: The numeric thresholds are from the city's description of the ordinance as proposed; the adopted text was not opened and may differ. Ordinance number not found. One outlet dates adoption June 3. City limits only.

sources.publisher: KUAR / UA Little Rock Public Radio

records.title: Proposed hyperscale data center moratoria (18-month, then six-month), both defeated
records.summary: The Board voted down an 18-month pause on hyperscale data center permits on August 4, 2026. A six-month version then failed on a 4-4 tie on October 20, so the June regulations remain the governing rules.
records.note: Vote dates inferred from the reports' references to Tuesday night. Both were sponsored by Director Kathy Webb; the 18-month version would have covered Google's planned Port of Little Rock project. News sources only.

records.title: Six-month pause on approving new data centers (July 2026)
records.summary: The city adopted a six-month pause on approving new data centers in July 2026 while it develops regulations.
records.note: Status date is the report date. Exact adoption date and tally were not in the source; six months from July 2026 puts expiry around January 2027. City limits only. News source only.

records.title: Planning commission denial of proposed cryptocurrency mining facility (April 2025)
records.summary: Vilonia's planning commission unanimously rejected a proposal for a crypto mining facility inside city limits after weeks of resident opposition. The same commission had denied an earlier mine in 2023.
records.note: Status date is the report date; the vote date, applicant and permit type were not in the source. Trade-press source only.

records.title: Clean and Reliable Grid Affordability Act (Public Act 104-0458, SB 25) - statewide county siting standards for energy storage, 55 ILCS 5/5-12024
records.summary: Sets statewide zoning standards for standalone commercial energy storage that zoned counties may not exceed, including 150-foot setbacks from nonparticipating homes and community buildings and 50 feet from property lines and road rights-of-way. Counties may not ban storage countywide or exclude it from every agricultural or industrial district, face hearing and permit deadlines and fee caps, and must bring their ordinances into line within 120 days of the effective date.
records.note: The statute text on ilga.gov could not be opened (TLS certificate error), so siting details come from a law-firm bulletin and a county State's Attorney memo. Standards bind counties; the opened sources do not address municipalities. One county memo puts the conformance deadline at 2026-09-29. The act also sets a 3,000 MW storage procurement target.

sources.publisher: Tazewell County (State's Attorney memo attached to Land Use Committee minutes)

records.title: Electric Vehicle Charging Act (765 ILCS 1085)
records.summary: Requires new single-family and small multifamily homes to have at least one EV-capable parking space per unit with parking, and parking at new or renovated large multifamily buildings to be EV-capable, with phased percentages for affordable housing starting in 2026. It also bars condominium associations from prohibiting owner-installed chargers and lets tenants install chargers at their assigned space at their own cost.
records.note: Source is a federal summary of state law, marked news because it is not the statute; ilga.gov could not be opened. Search results list this as Public Act 103-0053 (SB 40), effective 2024-01-01, but those pages were not opened, so the dates are left null. The same summary notes that an entity selling electricity solely for EV charging is not a public utility (220 ILCS 5/3-105).

sources.publisher: U.S. Department of Energy, Alternative Fuels Data Center

records.title: POWER Act (House Bill 5513 and Senate companion) - data center energy, water and community requirements
records.summary: Introduced 2026-02-11, the bill would make large new data centers pay for their own energy and supporting infrastructure, source renewable power, report and permit water use, and enter community benefits agreements. It did not get a vote before the spring 2026 adjournment, and sponsors said negotiations would continue toward the fall veto session.
records.note: News only. The House bill number comes from the article's ILGA link, not its text; the Senate bill number was not confirmed in an opened source. Outcome of the fall 2026 veto session not verified.

records.title: Senate Bill 1050 - local government standards and public hearing for data centers
records.summary: Would let local governments set standards for data-center size, design and location and would require a public hearing before a local vote. It did not pass in the spring 2026 session and was reported as expected to return in the fall veto session.
records.note: News only; bill number and description are as reported, not checked on ilga.gov. The same article cites House Bill 5755, which would send data-center proposals to local referendum.

records.jurisdiction: State of Illinois (Governor / Department of Commerce and Economic Opportunity)
records.title: Governor's directive pausing new Data Center Investment Program agreements
records.summary: After the legislature adjourned without acting on data centers, the Governor directed DCEO to stop processing new Data Center Investment Program tax-incentive agreements from 2026-07-01. Agreements signed before that date are honored, and he asked lawmakers to take up a broader framework on rates, water, clean energy and transparency.
records.note: The official press release was read as reposted by a news site, not on illinois.gov. No end date stated. Whether the fall 2026 veto session changed this was not verified.

sources.publisher: Capitol Fax (reposting the Governor's press release)

records.title: ICC order approving ComEd large-load deposit tariff (docket 25-0677)
records.summary: The commission approved ComEd's request to scale security deposits for new large-load projects such as data centers to requested capacity, replacing a flat one-million-dollar deposit. It also directed staff to open a further proceeding on additional ratepayer protections.
records.note: News only. statusDate is the report date; the order issued the Thursday before. Deposits reportedly start at 1 million dollars for 50-200 MW requests and rise 500,000 dollars per additional 100 MW. Does not apply to data centers already connected. The docket number is taken from the article's link (P2025-0677). ComEd territory only; outcome of the follow-on proceeding not verified.

records.title: 12-month moratorium on large-scale data center development
records.summary: The county board approved a one-year pause on data centers with at least 10,000 square feet of processing area, lengthening a nine-month pause set in committee. It ends early if the county finalizes a zoning and permitting ordinance sooner.
records.note: News only. The article does not spell out the boundaries; county zoning generally reaches only unincorporated land, and the task force is focused on unincorporated areas.

records.title: Resolution establishing a moratorium on battery energy storage systems
records.summary: The county board adopted an open-ended moratorium on battery storage facilities, including batteries proposed alongside solar and wind projects. No end date was set.
records.note: News only. Public Act 104-0458, effective 2026-06-01, bars county bans on storage in agricultural and industrial districts and required conforming ordinances by about 2026-09-29, so this moratorium may no longer be enforceable. Current status not verified.

records.title: Zoning approval for CyrusOne data center campus in Talkington Township
records.summary: The county board voted 17-10 to grant zoning approval for a 500-million-dollar CyrusOne campus on about 280 acres of farmland near Waverly, expected to draw about 600 megawatts at full build. Opponents had asked for a local moratorium, which the board did not adopt.
records.note: News only. The article calls the approval a zoning change or variance; other reports call it a conditional use permit. Construction permits were still required.

records.title: Land Use Committee discussion of data center zoning and a BESS ordinance
records.summary: Staff told the committee the zoning code does not address data centers and that they would draft rules limiting them to industrial areas; a member asked whether a moratorium was an option. Staff also plan one renewable-energy ordinance covering battery storage that references the national fire code for storage, written to fit the new state siting law. No action was taken.
records.note: Draft minutes, marked subject to committee approval. Discussion only; no ordinance or moratorium adopted as of that meeting.

records.title: Washington County Battery Energy Storage Systems Ordinance
records.summary: The county-posted text limits storage above 600 kWh to agricultural or industrial districts by special use permit. It sets setbacks of 1.5 miles from municipal limits, 200 feet from parcel lines and roads, 600 feet from nonparticipating homes and 1,000 feet from hazardous facilities, with a 35-foot height cap, decommissioning security and sizeable application and operating fees.
records.note: The file is labelled Final on the county site but carries no adoption date, ordinance number or signatures, so adoption is not confirmed and status is recorded as proposed. Its setbacks and fees exceed the caps in Public Act 104-0458 for counties, so check what is currently enforceable.

records.title: Resolution 26-4609 asking the General Assembly to restore county siting authority over solar, wind and battery facilities
records.summary: The county board's Legislative Committee unanimously approved a resolution urging the state to repeal or amend the laws that limit county zoning over commercial solar, wind and battery storage, including Public Act 104-0458. The full board still had to vote.
records.note: News only, from a small local outlet. An advocacy resolution with no regulatory effect; full-board outcome not verified.

records.title: Data center regulations (Ordinances O26-021 through O26-024)
records.summary: Every new data center now needs a conditional use permit with a public hearing and council approval, plus verified sound, water and energy studies; evaporative cooling and modular nuclear are prohibited. New facilities must either generate a quarter of peak load from on-site renewables or install battery storage sized to half of peak load for 15 minutes, and all data centers face annual energy, water and noise reporting.
records.note: The city's news release gives the council vote as 2026-03-24; its zoning page says the rules were adopted 2026-03-25. Effective date not stated. BESS is tagged because on-site storage is a compliance path, not because storage siting is regulated. City limits only.

records.title: Ordinance O25-064: 180-day moratorium on new data center and warehouse developments
records.summary: Council enacted a 180-day pause on new data-center and warehouse developments in September 2025. It ended when the new data-center regulations were adopted in March 2026.
records.note: The city says the moratorium was set to lapse 2026-03-23 and a one-time 30-day staff extension was invoked before the regulations passed. Superseded by the record above.

records.title: Six-month moratorium on data center projects of 5 MW or more
records.summary: Council unanimously approved a six-month pause during which the city will not accept applications for data centers using five megawatts or more. Staff are to study impacts and draft regulations in the meantime.
records.note: News only, from a regional radio site. statusDate is the report date; the vote date is not stated. Six months would run to roughly late November 2026; extension or replacement rules not verified.

records.title: Mayoral Executive Order 2026-5: enhanced review of data centers
records.summary: Data-center projects that need a new Planned Development now get multi-agency review of power, water, backup generation, emissions, noise and community impacts, effective immediately. City departments must deliver permit conditions, air and noise rules and draft code amendments on set deadlines running to March 2027, and the order asks City Council to enact a moratorium.
records.note: Law-firm summary; the order itself was not opened. statusDate is the publication date; the signing date (early August 2026) is not stated in the opened source. No numeric MW threshold in the order.

records.title: Proposed 12-month data center moratorium ordinance
records.summary: The mayor introduced an ordinance, cosponsored by three aldermen, that would block new data centers in the city for one year. No council vote on it was reported.
records.note: News only. A search-result headline (not opened) suggests the moratorium later stalled in council, so treat it as not in force. A separate ordinance requiring data centers to report water and energy use was set for a final vote the same day; its outcome was not verified.

records.title: 12-month moratorium on cryptocurrency mines and data centers
records.summary: Council voted 5-0 for a 12-month moratorium on applications, permitting and permit approvals for cryptocurrency mines and data centers.
records.note: News only. Applies in city limits and the 1.5-mile extraterritorial area.

records.title: Data center moratorium (developments over 21,780 square feet)
records.summary: Council passed a moratorium under which the city will not accept applications for new data centers larger than about half an acre of floor area. It renews each year until council votes to change or end it.
records.note: statusDate is the city's post date; the vote was the Tuesday night before. Covers the city plus the area up to 1.5 miles outside city limits where the city has zoning authority. Existing businesses may continue.

records.title: Denial of Karis Critical data center at the former Lucent campus
records.summary: Council voted 6-1, with two abstentions, to deny a roughly 145,000-square-foot data center proposed along the I-88 corridor. A developer offer to halve the number of diesel backup generators did not change the outcome.
records.note: News only. A project-specific denial, not an ordinance; it signals council posture on data centers near homes.

records.title: Ordinance 26-O-0011: 180-day moratorium on data center and battery energy storage applications
records.summary: Council voted 12-0 for a 180-day pause on new permits and approvals for data centers and battery energy storage facilities while the city decides whether more regulation is needed.
records.note: Source is a local newsletter, not the city or a major outlet. A Daily Herald item seen only in search results refers to a July 20 moratorium date, so confirm the adoption and effective dates with the city. A later ordinance granting an exception was reportedly discussed in August 2026.

records.title: Temporary ban on EV charger installations in parking garages
records.summary: The mayor and village board approved a temporary ban on installing EV charging stations inside parking garages and structures. It followed a January 2024 vehicle fire during charging at a mall garage that took hours to put out.
records.note: News only. statusDate is the article's update date; the vote date, legal instrument and duration are not stated. Reported as applying to parking structures, not surface lots. Current status not verified.

records.title: Ordinance 2026-011 amending Title 11 to establish zoning regulations for electric vehicle charging stations
records.summary: The text allows EV chargers as an accessory use in parking lots and structures wherever the principal use is permitted, and requires special use approval in business or industrial districts for a site whose primary use is charging. It adds standards for permits, circulation, signage, maintenance, accessibility and compliance with the state EV Charging Act.
records.note: The opened copy is the meeting-packet version pre-dated for adoption on 2026-04-06, with a blank roll call and no signatures, so adoption is not confirmed and status is recorded as proposed. The Plan Commission hearing was 2026-03-11.

records.title: SB 167 (2025) - no ratepayer recovery of utility EV charging station costs
records.summary: Would have barred electric public utilities from recovering EV charging station costs from ratepayers and required them to set EV charging service rate schedules. It had a Senate Utilities hearing on February 11, 2025 and went no further.
records.note: 'Expired' means the Legislature's page marks it Died in committee. SB 380 (2026) is the narrower measure that became law.

records.title: SB 380 (2026 Session Laws ch. 120) - utility-owned public fast charging
records.summary: A retail electric supplier that owns or operates a public fast charging station (50 kW DC or more) must offer fair, reasonable and nondiscriminatory rates and services to all charging providers. It may not give its own stations an unreasonable competitive advantage.
records.note: Takes effect on publication in the statute book. Exempts utility stations built or operated before July 1, 2026, fleet and employee-only stations, and stations required by law or KCC order.

records.title: SB 417 / HB 2636 (2026) - KCC permitting, setbacks and county approval for industrial wind, solar and battery storage
records.summary: Would have required a KCC permit before building or expanding industrial battery storage (1 MWh or more), wind or solar, with minimum setbacks, decommissioning assurance and registration of existing facilities. County commissions could permit or deny projects, subject to a protest petition and election.
records.note: 'Expired' means both bills are marked Died in committee. Requested for the Kansas Farm Bureau and Kansas Livestock Association, so a refiled version in 2027 is plausible.

records.title: SB 526 (2026) - zoning condition on the data center sales tax exemption
records.summary: Would have limited the qualified data center sales tax exemption to facilities on land zoned industrial or manufacturing, or unzoned as of July 1, 2025. It did not advance past introduction.
records.note: 'Expired' means the Legislature's page marks it Died in committee, with no action dates.

records.title: SB 531 (2026) - no new large-load data centers in recent drought-emergency counties
records.summary: Would have prohibited developing or operating any new large-load data center in a county with a drought emergency declared in the previous three years. It did not advance past introduction.
records.note: 'Expired' means the Legislature's page marks it Died in committee, with no action dates. Requested by Sen. Murphy.

records.title: SB 98 (2025) - 20-year sales tax exemption for qualified data centers
records.summary: Gives a 20-year state and local sales tax exemption to data center projects investing at least $250 million within five years and creating 20 jobs. Projects must agree to efficient water use and to buy power for 10 years from the certified local utility; electricity is not exempt.
records.note: Signed in April 2025; exact day not shown on the pages opened. Still in force after the 2026 session, where a bill to narrow it (SB 526) died.

records.title: Evergy Large Load Power Service (LLPS) rate plan approved
records.summary: The KCC approved a unanimous settlement creating a rate plan for Evergy customers with peak load of about 75 MW or more. It requires a 12-year minimum term plus up to five ramp years, a minimum bill at 80 percent of contract demand, two years of collateral, exit fees and direct assignment of upgrade costs.
records.note: The release does not print the docket number; it is commonly cited as 25-EKME-315-TAR, which I did not verify. Applies in Evergy's Kansas territories only.

records.title: De facto hold on data centers, crypto mining and BESS pending a zoning text amendment
records.summary: The county has no formal moratorium. Staff say they will not act on applications for data centers, crypto facilities or battery storage until a text amendment begun in 2024 is written, with BESS rules to be drafted first.
records.note: News only. No draft code or timeline as of the May 6, 2026 work session. County zoning jurisdiction only; Lawrence was separately being asked for a moratorium.

records.title: Commission discussion of a three-year data center moratorium
records.summary: The commission chair said commissioners want a three-year moratorium on data center development in place while they do due diligence. No vote was reported.
records.note: News only. I could not confirm whether a resolution was later adopted.

records.title: Resolution 2026-10 - temporary moratorium on commercial battery energy storage systems
records.summary: Stops the county from acting on conditional or special use permits and construction permits for commercial battery storage in unincorporated areas until June 11, 2027. It directs a comprehensive plan update and zoning text amendments.
records.note: Does not apply to non-commercial systems for a property owner's own use. Can be extended, ended early or amended by later resolution.

records.title: Moratorium on data center construction through 2028
records.summary: Commissioners approved a resolution pausing data center construction through the end of 2028 while planning staff draft regulations. The county said it had no rules for data centers or crypto mining.
records.note: News only; vote date inferred from a January 14, 2026 article. A separate July 2025 county moratorium on battery storage until January 1, 2028 is widely reported, but I could not open a source for it.

records.title: Resolution No. 2026-R10 - moratorium on commercial battery energy storage permits
records.summary: Suspends consideration and issuance of special use permits or other zoning changes for commercial battery storage (1 MW or more over one hour) in the unincorporated area for 18 months. The county is to consider zoning amendments during that time.
records.note: Runs 18 months from publication in the official county newspaper, so roughly to August 2027; exact date not shown. The board can shorten or extend it.

records.title: 90-day moratorium on data center development (not extended)
records.summary: Commissioners imposed a 90-day moratorium on data center development on May 13, 2026 by a 3-2 vote. On August 5 a motion to extend it through January 31 failed 3-2 and it lapsed, leaving data centers under the special use permit process.
records.note: News only; unincorporated areas. Unverified search results suggest new short moratoria on data centers and battery storage in September 2026. Check county records before treating the county as open.

records.title: 12-month moratorium on data centers, battery storage and crypto mining
records.summary: The commission unanimously adopted a temporary 12-month moratorium on new applications and permits for data processing centers, battery energy storage and cryptocurrency mining facilities in unincorporated areas.
records.note: News only. The article prints May 11 without a year; 2026 is inferred from the weekday. Twelve months would end about May 2027.

records.title: Moratorium on data center applications in unincorporated areas (extended)
records.summary: Commissioners extended the county's moratorium on data center applications in unincorporated areas to June 1, 2027. In February 2026 they had also agreed in principle to a one-year pause covering battery storage, but I found no confirmed adoption of that part.
records.note: News only. The extension vote date is inferred as Monday, May 11, 2026 from a May 13 article. Treat BESS as unverified here.

records.title: Moratorium on commercial battery energy storage systems
records.summary: Commissioners adopted a moratorium on commercial battery energy storage in late July 2025, first reported as running through January 2028. On February 2, 2026 they approved a resolution setting the battery and hydrogen storage moratorium to run to September 1.
records.note: News only. The two reports conflict on the end date (January 2028 vs. September 1, year inferred as 2026). The September date has passed and I found no later extension or adopted rules, so treat current status as unknown.

records.title: Moratorium on new data centers in unincorporated areas (extended)
records.summary: The county adopted a six-month moratorium on new data centers in unincorporated areas in summer 2025. On February 2, 2026 it approved a resolution extending it to December 1.
records.note: News only. The extension article gives December 1 without a year; 2026 is inferred. Existing data centers and those inside city limits are unaffected.

records.title: Proposed bans on BESS and hyperscale data centers defeated
records.summary: At a special session the commission voted down, 2-3 each, a ban on battery energy storage and a ban on hyperscale data centers over one acre in zoned unincorporated areas. No moratorium or new rules were adopted, so applications are reviewed case by case.
records.note: News only; the county's own summary returned 403. Meeting date inferred as Monday, June 15, 2026. Resident petitions for a ban continued afterward.

records.title: Denial of Mountain Peak Energy Storage (Plus Power) 350 MW / 1,400 MWh BESS
records.summary: The commission voted 4-1 to deny a 350 MW battery storage project at McReynolds and Simpson Roads after neighbors filed a valid protest petition. Commissioners cited fire response and safety concerns and constituent opposition.
records.note: News only. A project denial, not an ordinance, but it shows how the commission treats large standalone storage.

records.title: Moratorium on data center, nuclear and hydrogen energy facilities in unincorporated areas
records.summary: The commission voted 4-0 to halt construction of data centers, nuclear power facilities and hydrogen-based energy facilities in unincorporated areas. It is set for three years, and commissioners can shorten or lengthen it.
records.note: News only; resolution number not found. A three-year term would run to about March 2029. Does not apply inside Salina or other cities.

records.title: Interim development control on battery energy storage zoning applications
records.summary: The county commission adopted a resolution pausing zoning applications where battery storage is the primary use, or an ancillary use of 600 kWh or more. It runs through March 11, 2027 or until BESS zoning provisions are adopted and published.
records.note: The 600 kWh ancillary threshold is low enough to catch commercial behind-the-meter batteries and solar-plus-storage. Vote tally not stated in the release.

records.title: Interim development control pausing data center applications
records.summary: Since January 14, 2026 the county has barred its planning department from accepting or considering data center applications while zoning rules are drafted. The third extension, on September 2, 2026, runs the pause through December 24, 2026.
records.note: News only. The sources do not say whether it reaches inside Wichita or other cities; assume county zoning jurisdiction. No data center regulations had been adopted as of September 2026.

records.title: Proposed six-month data center moratorium denied
records.summary: The council voted 3-2 to deny a six-month moratorium on applications for facilities whose primary use is a data center. Days earlier the planning commission had denied a proposal to convert a Logistics Park Kansas City warehouse into a data center.
records.note: News only. Vote date inferred as Thursday, June 11, 2026 from a June 16 article. No moratorium is in place; projects are decided case by case.

records.title: Voter-approved 10-year ban on high-impact data centers and Tier 2 and 3 battery energy storage
records.summary: Voters approved an initiative ordinance imposing a 10-year ban on high-impact data centers and Tier 2 and Tier 3 battery storage, by roughly 3,000 to 1,200 in unofficial results. The city commission cannot amend or repeal it; changes need another public vote.
records.note: News only; results unofficial pending canvass. The ordinance text and its definitions were not read, and the effective date is not reported. A separate commission moratorium ran to November 30, 2026. City limits only.

sources.publisher: The Cool Down (citing The Wichita Eagle)

records.title: Voter-approved 10-year bans on high-impact data centers and Type 2 and 3 BESS (enforcement awaiting court ruling)
records.summary: Voters approved a 10-year ban on high-impact data centers (4,346 to 2,891) and one on Type 2 and Type 3 battery storage (4,067 to 3,117) in unofficial results. A Lyon County judge has not ruled on the petition's validity, and the ordinance cannot be enforced until then.
records.note: News only. If the court finds the petition administrative, the measures may be void. The city also says the ordinance cites a code section that does not exist. City limits only.

records.title: Proposed six-month data center moratorium denied
records.summary: The council considered and denied a six-month moratorium on data centers. The request followed a developer withdrawing its application after community pushback.
records.note: News only; vote tally not reported.

records.title: Ameren Missouri large-load customer tariff (SB 4 implementation)
records.summary: The PSC unanimously approved Ameren Missouri's tariff for customers of 75 MW or more. It includes a 12-year minimum service term, exit fees, a two-year notice to leave or reduce load, optional clean-energy subscription programs and annual compliance reports.
records.note: The case number was not stated in the sources opened. The PSC fact sheet confirms Ameren and Evergy both have approved large-load tariffs and lists the common terms (collateral, 80% minimum demand charge).

records.title: Case EO-2025-0154: Evergy Missouri Metro / Missouri West Large Load Power Service tariff, Report and Order
records.summary: The PSC approved Evergy's large-load service class for customers at or above 75 MW, implementing SB 4. It sets eligibility, pricing and commitment terms meant to make large loads such as data centers cover their own costs.
records.note: PSC staff and the Office of Public Counsel did not support the order, per news coverage. Later rehearing and compliance-tariff filings were not opened.

records.title: Case ET-2026-0184: Liberty Utilities large-load tariff
records.summary: Liberty, the third regulated electric utility in Missouri, has a large-load tariff case in progress before the PSC, which was taking public comment.
records.note: The fact sheet is undated (file metadata shows late March 2026). The outcome since then was not checked.

records.title: HB 2062 (2024), RSMo 67.288: limits on local EV charging station mandates
records.summary: Bars cities and counties from requiring EV charging stations, or wiring for future ones, on parking lots owned or leased by churches and nonprofit organizations. Property and business owners may still install chargers voluntarily.
records.note: The preemption covers church and nonprofit lots only; local EV-ready rules for other properties are not preempted. Signing date not confirmed in an opened source; the August 28, 2024 date is what AFDC lists.

sources.publisher: U.S. DOE Alternative Fuels Data Center

records.title: HB 2239 (2026): AI Data Center Environmental Accountability Act
records.summary: Would have required AI data centers of 100 MW or more, built or expanded after August 28, 2027, to use closed-loop or equivalent low-water cooling and file annual environmental and health reports with the Department of Natural Resources, with penalties up to $50,000 a day. It received no hearing.
records.note: Status date is the end of the 2026 session as reported by the news source.

records.title: HB 2609 (2026): electric vehicle charging station requirements
records.summary: Would have made any city or county that mandates EV chargers pay to install, maintain and operate them, capped mandates at five chargers per lot, and exempted lots of 30 or fewer spaces.
records.note: Bill content is from the House summary. The expired status is inferred: the news source confirms only that the session ended May 15, 2026 and does not mention this bill. A third-party tracker (not cited) listed it as died in committee; the official House bill page could not be opened.

records.title: HB 3362 / HB 3364 (2026): use of resources by industrial users
records.summary: Would have required municipal utilities and cooperatives to adopt tariffs for customers of 50 MW or more, required load-shedding plans that protect residential and critical service, and required a state permit for withdrawing more than 2 million gallons of water a day. Neither bill reached the House floor.
records.note: Only the HB 3362 summary was opened; the news source says HB 3364 (Costlow) is identical. Sponsors have said they intend to refile next session.

records.title: SB 1750 (2026): regulation of large load electric customers
records.summary: Would have lowered the large-utility tariff threshold from 100 MW to 50 MW. It also would have required owners of large load facilities (data centers) to file a disclosure of intent to operate with the PSC before operating after August 28, 2026.
records.note: The news source reports that Sen. McCreery's data center bill got no hearing before the session ended May 15, 2026, but does not give a bill number. Matching it to SB 1750 is an inference from the sponsor and subject.

records.title: SB 4 (2025) utility omnibus: large-load customer tariff schedules, RSMo 393.130.7
records.summary: Electric utilities with more than 250,000 customers must file tariff schedules for customers projected to exceed 100 MW of annual peak demand (50 MW for smaller utilities). The schedules must make those customers pay their share of the cost to serve them and keep unjust costs off other customer classes.
records.note: Signing date is from the governor's release, which does not mention the large-load provision; that language was read in the truly-agreed bill text. Effective date not confirmed in the sources opened.

records.title: Six-month data center moratorium (in litigation)
records.summary: Commissioners signed a six-month moratorium on data centers on August 10, 2026. A developer sued, and a judge granted a temporary restraining order on September 8 and extended it on September 21 while weighing a preliminary injunction.
records.note: This is Benton County, Missouri, not Arkansas. Enforcement was under a restraining order as of September 21, 2026, and the final ruling was not found. News source only.

records.title: 12-month moratorium on large solar, wind, battery storage and data center developments
records.summary: Commissioners imposed a 12-month pause on larger new solar, wind, battery storage and data center projects outside city limits, extendable once by up to six months. Small on-site systems and existing projects are exempt.
records.note: The small-system exemption appears to be 25 kW but the report does not define it fully. No specific project was pending. News source only.

records.title: 180-day moratorium on processing data center and BESS land use applications
records.summary: The County Legislature voted 8-0 to pause processing of land use applications for data centers and battery energy storage systems for 180 days while it writes permanent code standards and public-notice rules.
records.note: The county executive's signature and the exact start and end dates were not in the sources; KCUR later reported it expires in December 2026. Sources do not say whether it reaches beyond unincorporated areas. It was first introduced in April 2026 as a 120-day pause.

records.title: Order and Ordinance enacting a temporary moratorium on data centers
records.summary: Commissioners unanimously imposed a six-month halt on building, converting, opening or expanding data centers of 2,500 sq ft or 250 kW and up in unincorporated areas. It covers crypto mining and supporting facilities such as substations, backup generation and battery storage serving a data center.
records.note: The PDF opened is the unsigned draft dated July 14, 2026; adoption on July 21 is confirmed by the news report. It runs six months from adoption (about January 21, 2027) and may be extended once by up to six months. Projects with foundation or vertical work already begun are exempt; grading alone does not count. The county has no zoning.

sources.publisher: Nodaway County Commission (draft order, hosted by KQ2)

records.title: Six-month moratorium on large-scale data centers
records.summary: The County Council unanimously barred approval of new or expanded large-scale data centers for six months. Large-scale means more than 100,000 square feet or more than 5 MW of demand.
records.note: Exact expiry not stated (roughly mid-January 2027). The source does not say whether it is limited to unincorporated areas. Council members have discussed renewing it or a permanent ban. News source only.

records.title: Draft data center zoning rules for unincorporated St. Louis County
records.summary: County planning staff presented draft rules that sort data centers into size tiers (micro under 10,000 sq ft and 3 MW, up to major over 250,000 sq ft and 50 MW). The draft restricts locations and sets light, sound and energy requirements for larger ones.
records.note: Draft only, covering unincorporated areas; a second draft was expected mid-September 2026 and the outcome was not checked. Status date is the report date. News source only.

records.title: Six-month moratorium on data centers, solar, wind and battery energy storage in unincorporated areas
records.summary: The County Commission adopted a temporary six-month moratorium on data centers, solar and wind energy systems and battery energy storage systems in unincorporated Webster County.
records.note: Exact end date not stated (roughly mid-December 2026). The county has no countywide zoning. The county says it does not affect the data center already under construction on Rifle Range Road.

records.title: Annexation, rezoning and project ordinance for $6 billion CRG data center
records.summary: The council annexed and rezoned several hundred acres in November 2025 and passed a project ordinance around March 30, 2026 for a hyperscale data center. Residents then sued the city and developer to void the approvals, voters replaced four council incumbents, and recall petitions were filed.
records.note: The March 30 date comes from a photo caption and the reference to an ordinance passed the week before April 10; exact vote dates and tallies were not in the sources opened. Litigation was pending. News sources only.

records.title: Six-month moratorium on new data center approvals and temporary ban on new battery storage sites
records.summary: The council voted 7-0 to halt new data center approvals for six months and, the same night, temporarily barred new battery energy storage sites. The Nebius project already under construction is not affected.
records.note: Vote date is inferred from the report's reference to Monday (article dated July 8, 2026). Permanent zoning rules were adopted October 5, 2026 (next record); sources do not say whether the moratorium was then lifted. City limits only.

records.title: Unified Development Ordinance amendments for data centers and battery energy storage systems
records.summary: The council unanimously required new data centers and BESS to sit at least 1,000 feet from homes, schools, parks, hospitals and similar uses. Data centers above 2.5 MW need a special use permit, and the rules add noise studies, decommissioning after 12 idle months and twice-yearly generator reports.
records.note: Setback variances are possible with planning commission recommendation and council approval. Ordinance number not given. City limits only. News source only.

records.title: City Plan Commission denial of 20-story Quality Hill data center (934 Central St.)
records.summary: The Plan Commission voted 6-0 against a proposed 384-foot downtown data center that would have replaced a historic building. Commissioners cited the location and limited benefit to the city.
records.note: The developer may ask the City Council to override; the mayor called a reversal highly unlikely. A separate ordinance creating a data center transparency task force was pending in committee. News source only.

records.title: Data center zoning code amendment (adopted January 15, 2026)
records.summary: The council unanimously gave data centers their own use categories. They are barred from residential, neighborhood and retail districts without rezoning or a special use permit, need special use permits in several other districts, and must supply utility will-serve letters. Noise and property-line distance rules apply in manufacturing districts.
records.note: Ordinance number not stated in the sources. The council also directed a study of environmental and utility-rate effects. News sources only.

records.title: Six-month moratorium on commercial or industrial developments of 60 acres or more
records.summary: The council unanimously paused rezonings, plats, site plans and building and grading permits for commercial or industrial developments of 60 or more acres for six months, to review land use and utility capacity.
records.note: Not data-center-specific, and the source says it does not directly reach the $6 billion data center proposed outside city limits, though the city controls wastewater that project might use. Vote date inferred from the report's reference to Monday. Six months from adoption falls about November 11, 2026; check whether it was extended. Local news source only.

records.title: 120-day administrative delay on data center development
records.summary: The council imposed a 120-day pause on data center development while staff study land use, utility, noise and air impacts. An extension into February 2027 and new code definitions (accessory, micro, and large-load at 5 MW or 10,000 sq ft) were set for a November 16, 2026 vote.
records.note: Status date is the report date; the vote date and tally were not stated. Expiry of November 17 is from the October report. The outcome of the November 16 extension vote is not yet known. A developer lawsuit over the delay was reported in search results but not verified in an opened source.

records.title: Bill 14085: data centers defined and prohibited
records.summary: The council voted 7-1 to define data centers as facilities whose primary use is data processing or storage, including AI computing and crypto mining, and to disallow them in the city. Ordinary merchandise warehouses are carved out.
records.note: Applies inside city limits only. News sources only; ordinance text was not opened.

records.title: One-year moratorium on applications for new or expanded data centers
records.summary: The council unanimously adopted a one-year pause on accepting applications to build or expand data centers, after a large proposed project drew public opposition and was withdrawn.
records.note: Applies inside city limits only. Marked expired because it was superseded by the permanent zoning ban adopted May 19, 2026 (next record). News source only.

records.title: Board Bill 49 (2026-2027): data center zoning regulations, new Zoning Code Section 26.77
records.summary: The Board of Aldermen passed 13-0 a zoning framework that classifies data centers by size, limits where they can locate, and imposes renewable-energy, light and sound requirements. It was sent to the mayor, who was expected to sign.
records.note: Marked pending because the mayor's signature, ordinance number and effective date were not confirmed in the sources opened. St. Louis is an independent city. The 120 MW Armory project proceeds under a separate conditional use permit.

records.title: PNM's stated intent to file a large-load tariff
records.summary: PNM told an interim legislative committee it plans to file a large-load tariff with the PRC later in 2026. It would include minimum revenue requirements, exit fees and other protections for residential ratepayers.
records.note: News source only. No docket number or filing was found as of this research.

records.title: PRC 2026 Report: Large Load Policy & Technical Analysis Survey
records.summary: A PRC report surveys how other states protect ratepayers from stranded costs when large loads fail to materialise, covering dedicated large-load tariffs, exit fees, collateral, line-extension policies and securitization. It says New Mexico currently handles such costs through conventional ratemaking and adopts no rule.
records.note: A study, not a rulemaking or order. The publication date is not stated; the file path suggests August 2026. The report's definition of large loads includes EV charging infrastructure.

records.title: PRC Case No. 25-00048-UT, PNM solar and battery storage resources for Meta's Los Lunas data center
records.summary: A PRC presentation to legislators reports that the commission approved this case on 18 December 2025. It covers 290 MW of solar and 268 MW of battery storage serving Meta's Los Lunas campus, which is supplied under special service contracts with PNM.
records.note: Approval date and megawatts come from PRC slide decks, not the final order. The order was not opened, so cost-allocation terms are unverified.

sources.publisher: New Mexico Public Regulation Commission (legislative committee handout)
New Mexico Public Regulation Commission (legislative committee handout)

records.title: PRC Docket No. 25-00082-UT, El Paso Electric rate case with proposed Large Load Tariff Schedules Rate No. 50 and 51
records.summary: El Paso Electric's New Mexico base-rate application proposes two new large-load tariff schedules and a replacement line-extension policy. The procedural order set a public hearing for 21 September to 2 October 2026.
records.note: statusDate is the procedural order date. No final order was found, so the outcome after the hearing is unverified. Tariff terms (demand thresholds, contract length) were not in the notice.

sources.publisher: New Mexico Public Regulation Commission (customer notice)

records.title: Announced 2027 bill for a statewide moratorium on large-scale data centers
records.summary: Four Democratic legislators said they will introduce a temporary statewide pause on new large-scale data center projects in the 2027 session while the state builds a framework for water, energy, ratepayer and community impacts. No bill has been filed, and the length and size threshold are undefined.
records.note: statusDate is the KSFR report date. Sponsors named are Reps. Cadena, Rubio and Chávez and Sen. Hamblen. No bill number exists yet.

records.title: HB 88 (2025), Electric Vehicle Charging Station Zoning Act
records.summary: Would have made EV charging stations a permitted use in every county and municipal zoning district, with administrative-only review limited to construction-code compliance and deemed approval after 30 business days. It also would have counted charging spaces toward minimum parking; it died in its first House committee.
records.note: Listed as Died (action postponed indefinitely) with no dated final action. The bill was introduced 2025-01-13.

records.title: HB 93 (2025), Advanced Grid Technology Plans, including the self-sourced power / qualified microgrid section (Laws 2025, ch. 93)
records.summary: Lets a person in New Mexico take electric service from a qualified microgrid (self-source generation of at least 20 MW that can run islanded) under an electric service agreement with a utility. Energy from such a microgrid is not counted as retail sales under the renewable portfolio statutes until 2035, and it must be net-zero carbon by 2045.
records.note: This is the provision later criticised by legislators as a microgrid loophole for data centers that generate their own power.

records.title: SB 235 (2026), Microgrid Oversight Act
records.summary: Would have put qualifying data-center microgrids under Public Regulation Commission oversight with clean-energy standards and annual reporting. A committee substitute passed the Senate 22-20 but the bill was never heard in the House and died.
records.note: Passed the Senate 2026-02-14 and was sent to House Judiciary 2026-02-15. The legislature lists it as Died (action postponed indefinitely) with no date, so statusDate is null.

records.jurisdiction: State of New Mexico (Construction Industries Commission)
records.title: 2021 International Energy Conservation Code adoption with EV charging requirements for new development
records.summary: The Construction Industries Commission adopted the 2021 energy code with added EV provisions for new developments, including multifamily and commercial. As reported, 5% of parking spaces must have chargers and a further 5% to 15% must be EV-ready.
records.note: News source only. statusDate is the article date, because the adoption date is not given. The article gives the effective date as Aug. 1; the year 2024 is inferred from its publication date. Check the percentages against the adopted code text.

records.title: Pledged executive-order moratorium on new large-scale data centers (Deb Haaland)
records.summary: As the Democratic nominee, Deb Haaland pledged to order a pause on new large-scale data center projects on taking office, lasting until the state adopts protections and enforcement, with an eight-point checklist for projects. She has since been declared the winner of the governor's race; no order has been issued.
records.note: This is a campaign pledge, not a measure. The article does not say whether projects already under way would be covered.

records.title: Resolution setting conditions for data centers that seek county incentives
records.summary: Commissioners voted 4-1 for a resolution that conditions county public funds or tax breaks for data centers on full water-use offsets and reuse, a move to fully renewable power within two years, and labor commitments. Privately financed projects are not covered.
records.note: News source only; the resolution number is not confirmed. It applies only to projects asking the county for incentives such as industrial revenue bonds. It is not a zoning rule or a moratorium.

records.title: Project Jupiter industrial revenue bond and Local Economic Development Act ordinances
records.summary: The county commission voted 4-1 for an industrial revenue bond ordinance of up to $165 billion and a companion LEDA ordinance for the Project Jupiter data center campus in Santa Teresa. The county holds title and leases the property back, with developer payments in lieu of taxes.
records.note: The approval was contested; Commissioner Chaparro dissented after trying to postpone it. Ordinance numbers are not in the sources. The developers are BorderPlex Digital Assets and Stack Infrastructure.

records.title: One-year moratorium ordinance on data centers and direct supporting infrastructure
records.summary: The commission voted 4-1 for an ordinance barring the establishment, construction, expansion or operation of data centers and their direct supporting infrastructure for one year while the county considers regulations. It was prompted by a proposed solar-powered data center near Hachita.
records.note: News source only. The vote date is inferred from 'Thursday' and the article date. No size threshold or geographic scope is stated.

records.title: 18-month moratorium ordinance on data center development
records.summary: The Board of County Commissioners unanimously adopted an 18-month pause on data center development, with a 1 MW threshold, lowered from the 100 MW first proposed. Amendments added environmental-justice and cumulative-impact provisions, monitoring, and at least two staff progress reports.
records.note: The county release (dated 2026-07-02) says the vote was Tuesday night, which is 2026-06-30. The ordinance number and exact effective and expiry dates are not stated.

records.title: Rancho Viejo Solar conditional use permit (AES), solar with battery energy storage
records.summary: After quasi-judicial hearings on 11 and 12 August 2025, the Board of County Commissioners voted 4-1 to grant the land-use permit for AES's 96 MW solar project with up to 48 MW of battery storage near Eldorado. Battery fire safety was the centre of the dispute, and opponents said they would appeal.
records.note: The exact vote date is not confirmed: the news report of 2025-09-02 says 'last week', while the county advisory confirms only the hearing dates. Permit conditions and any later appeal are unverified.

records.title: Resolution opposing large-scale data centers, amended to include an 18-month moratorium
records.summary: The commission voted 3-0 for a resolution opposing large-scale data centers, amended at the meeting to add an 18-month moratorium for impact studies and regulatory planning.
records.note: News source only. It was adopted as a resolution, not an ordinance, and gives no size threshold. It does not apply to state land, so the proposed Spaceport America data center is not directly covered. The vote date is inferred from the article's publication date.

records.title: One-year moratorium on data centers and related infrastructure
records.summary: Commissioners unanimously approved a one-year bar on data center development on unincorporated county land and began forming a Blue Ribbon advisory committee to recommend regulations. The county currently has no zoning regulations.
records.note: News sources only. They do not say whether the measure is an ordinance or a resolution. It does not cover land inside the City of Socorro.

records.title: Proposed temporary moratorium on data center projects
records.summary: City commissioners considered a temporary data center moratorium but delayed the vote over possible legal conflicts with a February 2026 memorandum of understanding. That agreement lets Atterix run a six-month feasibility study for a data center project.
records.note: News source only and undated; other coverage places the postponement in June 2026. No adoption was found. Applies only inside city limits.

records.title: House Bill 15 (136th General Assembly) - energy law, including mercantile customer self-power systems
